name: Kicksecure
summary: A security-hardened Linux distribution based on Debian Stable, engineered with defense-in-depth protections, user-sysmaint isolation, torified system updates, and extensive kernel hardening.

content.introduction: Kicksecure is an open-source, security-hardened Linux distribution engineered to provide a robust defense-in-depth computing baseline against malware, remote exploitation, privilege escalation, and physical compromise. Created and coordinated by Patrick Schleizer (the founder of Whonix), Kicksecure translates the principles of the Securing Debian Manual and the Kernel Self Protection Project into an automated, turnkey operating system. Rather than attempting to deliver full-system traffic anonymization by default, Kicksecure focuses on local operating system hardening, software supply chain security, and strict account isolation for general-purpose computing.
content.what_is_it: Technically, Kicksecure is built upon the Debian GNU/Linux Stable foundation (Debian 12 Bookworm in the 17.x series, transitioning to Debian 13 Trixie in the 18.x series). It supplements the standard Debian userland with modular hardening packages, including `security-misc` (kernel sysctl hardening, module blacklisting, console lockdown), `tirdad` (TCP Initial Sequence Number randomization to prevent CPU information leaks), `sdwdate` (TLS/Tor-authenticated time synchronization), SUID permission reduction, and `open-link-confirmation`. Kicksecure functions as both a standalone desktop operating system and the upstream hardened foundation powering Whonix.
content.origin_and_history: Kicksecure originated around 2018–2019 as an effort within the Whonix project to decouple host and workstation hardening routines from Tor-specific network routing. Historically, security enhancements developed for Whonix-Workstation were tightly coupled to anonymizing proxies. Patrick Schleizer and the development team recognized that general Linux users required a hardened, non-torified desktop OS for everyday computing. The hardening components were modularized into independent Debian packages, culminating in the formal launch of Kicksecure as an independent distribution with dedicated ISO installation media, virtual machine appliances, and package repositories.
content.governance_and_whonix_relationship: Kicksecure is developed and governed by Patrick Schleizer and the Kicksecure/Whonix development team. Operating as a free software community initiative, the project publishes all source code, packaging recipes, and development discussions openly on GitHub (`github.com/Kicksecure`) and the official community forums. Funding is maintained through community donations, non-profit sponsorships, and user contributions. Kicksecure shares core engineering infrastructure with Whonix, serving as the common hardened upstream operating system layer that Whonix builds upon.
content.user_sysmaint_split_and_account_isolatio: A central structural security innovation in Kicksecure is the `user-sysmaint-split` model. Traditional desktop Linux systems grant the primary daily user account direct administrative access via passworded `sudo`. Kicksecure enforces a separation between the unprivileged daily workspace user and a dedicated system maintenance account (`sysmaint`). Daily user applications with high exposure surfaces (such as web browsers or office suites) cannot directly invoke administrative commands, mitigating the deployment of user-space rootkits and unauthorized persistence mechanisms.
content.torified_apt_updates_and_software_integr: While Kicksecure is intended for standard clearnet internet usage, it enforces a specialized network policy for software management: all default APT package manager update repositories are torified. Package index downloads and package installations occur exclusively over the Tor network. This architecture prevents upstream package mirror operators and local network eavesdroppers from identifying the user's real IP address or delivering targeted, malicious updates tailored to a specific user's known package inventory.
content.kernel_hardening_and_security_misc: Kicksecure deploys `security-misc`, a comprehensive hardening package implementing recommendations from the Kernel Self Protection Project (KSPP). It configures restrictive sysctl parameters, disables kernel information leak vectors (`dmesg` restrictions, `hidepid=2` for `/proc` filesystem mounting), blacklists obsolete or dangerous kernel modules (FireWire, Thunderbolt, legacy networking protocols), enforces a restrictive default `umask` (027) for non-root users, and locks down console access against brute-force authentication attacks.
content.tirdad_and_sdwdate_mitigations:
Kicksecure integrates specialized utilities to counter advanced network fingerprinting:

- `tirdad`: A custom Linux kernel module that randomizes TCP Initial Sequence Numbers (ISN), preventing remote adversaries from determining CPU activity cycles or correlating connections across different interfaces.
- `sdwdate`: Secure Distributed Web Date, an authenticated time synchronization daemon that fetches time over TLS and Tor connections from trusted servers. This completely replaces unauthenticated Network Time Protocol (NTP) daemons, eliminating time-spoofing attacks that desynchronize cryptographic validation.
content.suid_disabler_and_permission_hardener: To mitigate local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities, Kicksecure executes the SUID Disabler and Permission Hardener (`permission-hardener`). This subsystem scans the operating system during package updates and strips the setuid (SUID) and setgid (SGID) permission bits from unnecessary binaries, replacing functionality with granular POSIX file capabilities where required. Consequently, security vulnerabilities in legacy system executables cannot be leveraged by unprivileged processes to gain root authority.
content.calamares_installer_and_full_disk_encryp: Kicksecure ISO installation media utilize the Calamares graphical installer configured with mandatory Full Disk Encryption (FDE) defaults backed by LUKS2. During installation, storage partitions are formatted with authenticated encryption, the unauthenticated recovery console in `dracut` is disabled, and single-user recovery mode is removed from the GRUB boot menu. These protections prevent an adversary with brief physical access from bypassing operating system authentication.
content.emergency_shutdown_and_ram_wiping:
Kicksecure incorporates defensive controls for physical compromise scenarios:

- Emergency Shutdown: A configurable hotkey trigger that forces an immediate power cutoff, bypassing normal shutdown delays.
- RAM Wipe (`ram-wipe`): A cryptographic memory sanitization script executed during reboot and shutdown sequences that overwrites volatile system RAM with pseudorandom data, neutralizing cold-boot attacks aimed at recovering encryption keys.
content.deployment_modes_bare_metal_vm_and_morph:
Kicksecure provides diverse deployment options:

- Bare-Metal ISO: Standard bootable installer for physical desktop and laptop workstations.
- Pre-configured Virtual Machines: Appliance images optimized for KVM and VirtualBox.
- Qubes OS Template: Official `qubes-template-kicksecure` packages providing a hardened guest template for Qubes AppVMs.
- Debian Morphing: Ability to transform a standard Debian Stable installation into Kicksecure by adding the Kicksecure repository and installing `kicksecure-cli` or `kicksecure-gui` metapackages.
content.threat_model_and_operational_limits:
Kicksecure documents the boundaries of its threat model:

- Clearnet Traffic: Kicksecure is not an anonymity network OS. Standard web browsing, email, and streaming traffic exit over clearnet using the local ISP connection unless the user manually launches a VPN or Tor Browser.
- Firmware Compromise: Kicksecure cannot defend against compromised motherboard BIOS, malicious Option ROMs, or hardware implants installed prior to OS execution.
- Memory Exploitation Limits: While kernel self-protection and SUID stripping mitigate privilege escalation, Kicksecure relies on Debian's standard memory allocators and does not embed hypervisor compartmentalization like Qubes OS.
content.privacy_and_telemetry: Kicksecure maintains a strict zero-telemetry policy. The operating system contains no telemetry reporting daemons, user tracking identifiers, or usage analytics services. Software updates downloaded over torified APT connections ensure repository queries cannot be correlated with user identities. The project also publishes a public Warrant Canary confirming the absence of secret governmental warrants or undisclosed security compromises.
advantages: Extensive defense-in-depth baseline automating hundreds of security recommendations from the Securing Debian Manual
user-sysmaint-split architecture separating daily unprivileged desktop usage from administrative system maintenance
Torified APT updates protecting against targeted malicious software delivery and IP tracking by package mirrors
Advanced network fingerprinting mitigations including tirdad (TCP ISN randomization) and sdwdate authenticated time synchronization
Automated SUID binary stripping and strict AppArmor profiles minimizing local privilege escalation vectors
Flexible deployment options spanning bare-metal ISO, KVM/VirtualBox VMs, Qubes OS templates, and Debian package morphing
Zero telemetry policy with public Warrant Canary verification
disadvantages: Does not route general web traffic through Tor by default, requiring separate tools for online anonymity
Hardened sysctl and kernel restrictions can occasionally conflict with niche third-party software or debugging tools
Limited out-of-the-box hardware acceleration on specialized GPU chipsets without proprietary firmware
Higher administrative overhead due to explicit separation of the sysmaint maintenance account
Monolithic Linux kernel architecture lacking hardware-enforced Xen hypervisor isolation
who_is_it_for: Privacy and security-conscious individuals seeking a hardened Debian-based desktop for daily computing
System administrators and developers requiring a tamper-resistant workstation for administrative and code management tasks
Qubes OS users deploying standalone or template virtual machines with reinforced internal security
Users looking to upgrade existing vanilla Debian installations to a hardened defensive configuration
who_is_it_not_for: Whistleblowers and activists requiring strict, amnesic Tor routing for all network traffic (better suited to Tails or Whonix)
Users requiring strict hardware-enforced hypervisor domain compartmentalization (better suited to Qubes OS)
Casual computer users seeking a plug-and-play multimedia desktop with proprietary drivers enabled by default

components.name: tirdad TCP ISN Randomization Module
components.note: Custom kernel module randomizing TCP Initial Sequence Numbers to prevent CPU activity and clock leakage.

components.name: sdwdate Authenticated Time Sync
components.note: Secure distributed web time synchronization daemon fetching timestamps over TLS and Tor without NTP.

components.name: SUID Disabler & Permission Hardener
components.note: System scanner revoking SUID/SGID execution bits from unnecessary system binaries to limit privilege escalation.

components.name: Torified APT Repository Subsystem
components.note: APT transport configuration routing package downloads and repository metadata queries through Tor onion circuits.

components.name: systemcheck Diagnostic Utility
components.note: Automated system auditing utility verifying disk encryption status, user account security, and service health.
